strengths: Addresses important practical problem of video understanding efficiency with strong empirical results (95% token compression with minimal accuracy loss across 6 benchmarks)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple benchmarks, baselines, ablations, and efficiency metrics (72% GPU memory, 23.9% latency reduction)
Sound technical design combining event-based retrieval with RL-based distillation; memory-aware compression respects semantic boundaries
Results demonstrate superiority over compression baselines (65% improvement over ByteVideoLLM, 31% over MovieChat) and competitive/superior performance vs. larger models
Reasonable reproducibility with implementation details, hyperparameter validation through ablations, and concrete experimental setup
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: event segmentation, cosine-similarity frame merging, and GRPO are all existing techniques; C-GRPO is primarily GRPO with added retention reward (incremental contribution)

Insufficient justification of key choices: only 5K training instances without data efficiency analysis; fixed top-k=3 across all benchmarks without sensitivity ablations; minimal performance differences for τ (41.34→42.20→41.40) despite claims of validation

Incomplete experimental analysis: missing ablations on retrieval sensitivity (varying k), embedding model choice, computational cost of VMR, failure modes on non-event-structured videos; reference to 'Appendix ??' indicates missing content
Weak generalization validation: trained/validated only on Qwen2.5-VL-3B; minimal architecture diversity in baselines; unclear transfer to different VLM designs

Unexplained efficiency gaps: 23.9% latency reduction is modest relative to 95% token reduction; 72.4% GPU memory reduction but only 11.1% end-to-end latency improvement suggests visual encoding (not LLM) is bottleneck; practical deployment benefit unclear

Methodological comparison concerns: arbitrary token matching (≈120 tokens) for spatial methods; VideoMME shows only 74% retention under extreme compression with limited analysis; inconsistent compression targets across baselines

Presentation issues: Figure 1 duplicated with different captions; unclear when VMR is applied (training/inference/both); hyperparameter m not specified; overstated claims (groundbreaking, exceptional) for incremental work

strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem of efficient video understanding with strong real-world efficiency gains (72% GPU memory, 23.9% latency reduction)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 diverse benchmarks covering both video reasoning and general understanding tasks
Strong empirical results achieving near-baseline performance (42.20 vs 42.21) with extreme token reduction (95%)
Thorough ablation studies examining τ parameter sensitivity, VMR effectiveness, and comparison with supervised fine-tuning baselines
Well-articulated motivation grounded in cognitive science principles (episodic memory, event segmentation)
weaknesses: Critical confounding between frame selection (VMR) and compression: Table 2 shows VMR alone provides +3.35 points (42.21→45.56), making it unclear how much C-GRPO compression contributes versus VMR's retrieval bias
Unfair baseline comparisons: only MARC uses VMR retrieval with top-k=3 selection; other baselines receive no such advantage. Missing critical experiment of MovieChat+VMR

Limited technical novelty: VMR combines standard event detection (Soucek & Lokoc 2024), contrastive retrieval, and cosine-similarity merging; C-GRPO is incremental modification of GRPO (Shao et al. 2024) with reward gating
Incomplete paper with missing appendix references ('Appendix ??') on pages 8-9, raising reproducibility concerns
Insufficient analysis of C-GRPO design: only 3 τ values tested without statistical significance; retention ratio definition (Eq. 6) somewhat tautological; no justification for top-k=3 hyperparameter
Substantial performance loss on long videos (VideoMME: 39.44 vs 53.55 baseline = 26% drop) with no mechanistic analysis of failure modes
Potential data leakage: training uses Video-R1-260K which may overlap with evaluation benchmarks; only 5K training instances with unclear composition
No statistical testing, confidence intervals, or significance tests provided despite benchmark size variations

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem with clear motivation: reducing computational overhead of VLMs on video while maintaining performance
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 diverse benchmarks with detailed comparisons against 3 compression baselines and thorough ablation studies
Strong empirical results: maintains near-baseline performance (42.20 vs 42.21) while using 95% fewer tokens, with substantial efficiency gains (72% GPU memory reduction, 23.9% latency reduction)
Well-presented technical approach with clear mathematical formulations and effective visualizations of the method architecture
Creative cognitive science grounding for VMR design, connecting event-based segmentation to episodic memory principles
Systematic experimental methodology including ablations on τ parameter, VMR components, and comparison with supervised fine-tuning baselines
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components are largely existing work (event segmentation from Soucek & Lokoc 2024, C-GRPO as incremental extension of GRPO with added compression reward, standard cosine similarity compression). Primary contribution is combining existing techniques rather than novel methods
Critical presentation issue: broken appendix reference ('Extensive analysis...can be found in Appendix ??') on page 8 regarding VideoMME results, indicating incomplete submission for a top-tier venue

Unfair experimental comparison: only MARC uses VMR for benchmark processing while baselines lack access to oracle-like frame retrieval. VMR provides privileged information for frame selection that training-free methods cannot access, making direct comparison problematic

Incomplete analysis of VMR contributions: computational cost of event segmentation and retrieval not accounted for in efficiency metrics; unclear whether improvements stem from compression quality or biased sampling toward important frames; effects of segmentation vs retrieval not disentangled
Performance degradation on long-form videos: VideoMME shows only 74% retention (26% drop) at 3.21% tokens, contradicting claims of 'nearly identical accuracy' which only hold for shorter videos

Limited hyperparameter exploration: only τ parameter ablated with 3 values tested; other critical hyperparameters (top-k retrieval, group size G, compression ratio ρ, memory window m) not explored or discussed, limiting understanding of robustness

Questionable design choices lack justification: compression reward function (Eq. 7) appears ad-hoc with no exploration of alternative functional forms; τ=0.6 claimed as 'balanced' without principled justification; retention ratio definition (Eq. 6) assumes reward comparability that may not hold across different generation patterns
Generalization concerns: all training conducted on Qwen2.5-VL-3B; other models tested only without MARC-specific training, unclear whether C-GRPO transfers to different architectures

Training data selection not explained: only 5K instances sampled from 260K dataset with unclear selection criteria; mixing of video and image data during training with unclear contribution to compression performance
Incomplete analysis: missing appendix content prevents verification of VideoMME results and detailed experimental procedures; unclear why certain design choices were made over alternatives

strengths: Strong empirical results: Achieves 42.20 mean accuracy (99.98% of 42.21 baseline) while reducing visual tokens by 95%, with 72% GPU memory reduction and 23.9% latency improvement across 6 benchmarks

Comprehensive evaluation: Tests on diverse benchmarks (VSI-Bench, VideoMMMU, MMVU, MVBench, TempCompass, VideoMME), with detailed ablation studies, failure case analysis, and fair baseline comparisons

Well-motivated approach: The retrieve-then-compress pipeline is intuitive, with VMR grounded in cognitive science principles (event segmentation, episodic memory), and C-GRPO thoughtfully designed with retention ratio feedback and correctness gating
Practical impact: Addresses real deployment challenges for video VLMs in resource-constrained environments with clear efficiency gains measured on actual hardware
Solid technical execution: Two-stage memory-aware compression respects VMR structure, retention ratio formulation is reasonable, and implementation details are thorough with plans for reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: VMR uses existing TransNet v2 event detection plus standard contrastive retrieval with minimal innovation; C-GRPO is essentially GRPO + one compression reward term; the retrieve-then-compress pipeline represents straightforward combination of existing ideas

Incomplete component analysis: Table 2 shows VMR alone achieves 45.56 vs 42.21 baseline (8% gain), but the paper inadequately explains why retrieval improves full-frame models or what constitutes 'query-relevant' clips beyond retrieval similarity

Test-time overhead unaccounted: Figure 5 efficiency measurements exclude VMR computational cost (event detection, embedding, nearest neighbor search), potentially understating actual latency; end-to-end timing including retrieval stage not reported

Significant performance degradation on long videos: VideoMME achieves only 74% retention (39.44 vs 53.55), contradicting abstract's 'nearly identical accuracy' claim; limitation inadequately addressed in main text and suggests method brittleness to video length

Methodological concerns: C-GRPO trained on only 5K samples with 63% image data that 'will not contribute to compression reward'; sparse correctness gating (Eq. 8) provides weak training signal early on; top-k=3 choice for VMR retrieval lacks justification or sensitivity analysis
Incomplete efficiency evaluation: Latency/memory measurements only on MMVU benchmark; no breakdown of VMR component costs; no measurement of actual compression stage execution time

Fair comparison questions: MovieChat/VidCom/ByteVideoLLM reproduced under artificially matched token budgets rather than their intended operating regimes; SFT baseline trained on different dataset (Video-R1-COT-165K vs Video-R1-260K)
Missing statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported; small performance differences lack significance testing; only single seed experiments

strengths: Addresses a practical and timely problem of efficient video processing in VLMs with real-world deployment benefits
Comprehensive evaluation across 6 diverse benchmarks with detailed profiling showing concrete efficiency improvements (72% GPU memory reduction, 23.9% latency reduction)
Provides extensive implementation details and ablation studies supporting reproducibility
Interesting cognitive science motivation for event-based video segmentation
Includes analysis of failure cases and dataset-specific performance variations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: VMR uses existing event segmentation + standard contrastive learning; memory-aware compression is incremental over MovieChat; C-GRPO is merely adding a single retention reward term (Eq. 7) to GRPO

Problematic evaluation methodology: VMR preprocessing is applied only to MARC during evaluation but not to baselines, making comparisons unfair. Table 2 reveals VMR alone achieves 45.56 vs MARC's 42.20, suggesting VMR—not C-GRPO—drives most improvements

Misleading main claim of 'nearly identical accuracy': The comparison (42.20 vs 42.21) is not fair because the baseline doesn't use VMR, fundamentally changing the input distribution. This obscures that MARC uses content-aware retrieval, not pure compression

Unfair baseline comparisons: MARC combines training (5K samples) + VMR preprocessing + C-GRPO against training-free methods. Proper comparison would train baselines on same data or apply VMR to all methods equally

Fundamental limitation on long videos: VideoMME shows only 74% retention (39.44 vs 53.55). The method fails when videos have >3 important clips, contradicting claims of robustness. For the most computationally challenging scenario, performance degrades significantly
Unclear contribution attribution: Ablations don't isolate VMR's gain (~8%) from C-GRPO's gain (~5% over SFT+VMR). The paper conflates retrieval-based selection with compression performance
Incomplete baselines: No comparison with other learned compression or RL-based methods. No evaluation of baselines with VMR access, which would likely improve their scores substantially

Limited C-GRPO novelty: Adding correctness-gated retention rewards to GRPO is straightforward engineering. Gating by correctness is standard practice in reward modeling. The τ parameter choice (0.6) lacks theoretical justification
Small training dataset (5K samples) with limited scaling analysis and no statistical significance testing despite claiming performance equivalence to baselines
Cognitive science motivation is somewhat superficial; episodic memory framing is more accurately described as content-aware clip selection

strengths: Addresses practically important problem with strong motivation for efficiency gains in video VLMs
Comprehensive evaluation across 6 diverse benchmarks with convincing empirical results (42.20 vs 42.21 mean with 95% token reduction)
Meaningful efficiency improvements (72% GPU memory reduction, 23.9% latency reduction) with real-world significance
Good ablation studies demonstrating contribution of individual components (VMR, C-GRPO, τ sensitivity)
Clear methodology with detailed implementation details and commitment to reproducibility
Thoughtful grounding in cognitive science principles for event-based segmentation, though implementation is standard
weaknesses: Critical fairness concern: Only MARC uses VMR during evaluation, while baseline compression methods are not evaluated with query-aware VMR enabled—making it difficult to isolate compression contribution from retrieval contribution
Limited technical novelty—individual components (event detection, contrastive retrieval, cosine merging, GRPO) are from existing work; C-GRPO's retention reward is a straightforward extension

Significant failure case on long videos: VideoMME performance drops to 74% of baseline with acknowledged root cause (top-k=3 discards critical information for 100+ clip videos) but no adequate solution proposed
Experimental setup concerns: only 5K training samples for C-GRPO (vs 10K for SFT baseline) making controlled comparison difficult; both training and evaluation use overlapping Video-R1 data sources

Missing ablation: unclear how much improvement in 1-frame setting comes from VMR vs C-GRPO independently; SFT+VMR performs worse than VMR alone (Table 2), suggesting complex interactions not fully explained
Ambiguous notation: retention ratio η definition unclear (rewards vs accuracies); relationship between teacher and student networks during training needs clarification
